why_how.text: Montana requires a vision test before issuing a driver license.
The stated vision standard is at least twenty over forty in one eye or better, with or without corrective lenses.
Wear required glasses or contact lenses whenever driving, even on a short trip.
Driving without corrective lenses required by the license can result in a citation.
Keep spare glasses in the vehicle in case the usual pair is lost or broken.
Avoid dark glasses or tinted contacts at night because they reduce the light available for seeing.
Side vision helps detect hazards, but mirrors and a sideways glance may still be needed to see them clearly.
Judging vehicle speeds and distances takes practice, especially for merging gaps and two-lane passing.
If night vision is difficult, limit nighttime driving to what is necessary and drive cautiously when it is unavoidable.
Horns, sirens and screeching tires can give an audible warning of danger.
A driver with hearing loss can adapt by relying more on vision and staying alert.

why_how.text: Fatigue can reduce vision and alertness, slow decisions and make falling asleep at the wheel more likely.
Begin a long trip rested after a normal night’s sleep rather than leaving already tired.
Before leaving, eat lightly instead of a large meal that may cause sleepiness.
On a long trip, stop for a break about every two hours or whenever a break is needed.
Allow enough time to complete a trip without rushing.
Avoid driving late at night when that is normally your sleeping time.
Do not drive while sleepy; stop to sleep or share the driving with another driver when possible.
Alcohol impairs judgment, reflexes, reaction time, clear vision and alertness needed for driving.
If you drink alcohol, do not drive, because even a single beverage can affect driving.
The amount and pace of drinking, body weight, food and general health can all affect impairment.
Alcohol can accumulate even when someone consumes only one drink per hour.
The handbook’s drink comparison uses one and one-half ounces of eighty-proof liquor, twelve ounces of commercial beer or five ounces of wine.
Craft beer and specialty drinks can contain more alcohol than the standard drink examples.
Arrange for a designated driver who does not drink, or use available public transportation or a cab.

why_how.text: Prescription and nonprescription medicines can impair driving.
Check a medicine’s label for driving-related warnings before taking it when you plan to drive.
A medicine warning about operating heavy machinery also means not driving a car or truck.
If unsure about a drug’s driving effects, ask a physician or pharmacist about side effects.
The handbook warns against mixing alcohol with other drugs because the combination can intensify impairment or add harmful side effects.
When illness makes driving unsafe, have someone else drive.
Before each drive, decide whether you are physically and mentally able to drive safely.
For epilepsy, the handbook calls for a physician’s written attestation that the condition is stable and unlikely to interfere with safe driving.
Ask the treating doctor whether a heart condition could affect safe driving.
Stress or strong emotions can reduce concentration and safe-driving ability.
If angry or excited, wait off the road until calm before driving.
Allow extra trip time when impatience might encourage speeding or risky driving.
